Chapter 17 · Example 17.4

[0,1] Game #12 folding + an unlimited raising ladder — the last finite-pot [0,1] game

One full street, folding allowed, no check-raise, but now an arbitrary number of bets and raises. X acts first; each raise can be re-raised, forever. The new character is Rₚ — a pot-dependent generalization of the golden ratio r that sets the ratio between each threshold and the next, generating an infinite cascade of value thresholds marching toward the nuts. As P→∞ it becomes the no-fold Game #6.

The raising ladder  (value thresholds → the nuts)

    Rₚ  vs. pot  (→ r = √2−1)

    Rₚ is the ratio between each value threshold and the next in the raising ladder (yₙ = Rₚ₊… · xₙ₋₁). It solves the recursion Rₚ = [(P+2)/(P+3)] / [2 + Rₚ₊₂·(P+4)/(P+5)] and climbs to the golden mean r = √2−1 as P→∞.
    Value of the game to Y — now resolved. At this pot:  (ex-showdown, exact sequence-form LP, raise-ladder capped at B bets with B grown until the value converges — it converges completely by B = 6, the cascade's geometric decay in action). As P→∞ it climbs to the no-fold Game #6's 1/16 + r/8 ≈ 0.1143 (LP at P=1000: 0.1128). The book declines to compute the finite-pot value; an earlier CFR attempt here failed validation and was withdrawn — the LP replaces it, gate-validated by reproducing Game #10 exactly at a 2-bet cap (G(Y) match to 10⁻⁷) and the cascade x₁→y₂→x₃→y₄ at P=2 (0.248 / 0.085 / 0.030 / 0.013). One surprise: at every finite pot the unlimited-raise value sits below Game #10's two-bet value (0.06696 vs 0.06824 at P=2) — the third bet is X's option, and it costs Y more than Y's fourth-bet option wins back.

    What the endless ladder changes

    Every equation from Game #10 survives except the one at y₂ — because Y can now be re-raised. The fix is that the key relation y₂ = R·x₁ keeps its form but R is no longer the fixed (1−α₂)/2; it becomes the pot-dependent Rₚ.

    Once you pass the second raise the game is self-similar: every two further bets repeat the same ratios into an ever-larger pot. So the value thresholds form a cascade x₁ → y₂ → x₃ → y₄ → … each ≈ Rₚ times the last, converging geometrically to the nuts.

    The lower structure is unchanged. Adding more bets moves Rₚ (and hence x₁) but not the relationships among the low thresholds, so y₁, x₁*, y₀, x₀ follow the same formulas as Game #10. And since there's no check-raise, x₁* = y₁* again.

    As P → ∞, Rₚ → r and x₁ → 1/(1+2r) ≈ 0.547: the exact solution of the no-fold Game #6, with its r-geometric threshold ladder.

    Model from Bill Chen & Jerrod Ankenman, The Mathematics of Poker, Example 17.4 (“[0,1] Game #12”: full street / folding / unlimited bets / no check-raise). Exact core: Rₚ solves Eq. near 17.14; x₁=(1−α)²/[1+α+(2−α)(1−α₂)Rₚ]; cascade yₙ=Rₚ·xₙ₋₁; lower thresholds as in Game #10. Verified at P→∞ against Game #6 (x₁→1/(1+2r), y₂→r·x₁).
